newsitem.title: SPAIN: New Spanish party aims to unite left-wing opposition.
newsitem.headline: New Spanish party aims to unite left-wing opposition.

text.p: A new Spanish left-wing party concluded its inaugural conference on Sunday promising to unite the left-wing opposition against the ruling conservative Popular Party (PP).

The New Left Democratic Party (PDNI), born from the ranks of the United Left (IU) coalition, told supporters during the three-day conference it would unite IU and forge closer links with the leading opposition Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE).

"The party was created to defend the plurality of IU which is under threat at the moment, and to develop relations with other political groups," PDNI chairman Cristina Almeida told Spanish newspaper El Pais.
Almeida is a member of parliament for the United Left.

Party delegates told the 10,000 supporters who attended the Madrid conference they would strengthen and revive left-wing politics in Spain to eventually oust the conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.
The PSOE's representative at the conference, parliamentary spokesman Joaquin Almunia, welcomed the new party.
"I want to tell you on behalf of the PSOE that as a political party, you will work with us and we will work with you," he told delegates.
IU leader Julio Anguita came under fire for failing to attend the conference but New Left leaders said they had no plans to break away from the Communist-led coalition.
"We are here to defend the IU. We are not here to fight the Communist party or the PSOE, we are a force that intends to unite and not divide," said party secretary Diego Lopez Garrido.
United Left, the third voice of Spanish politics, won 11 percent of the vote in a general election in March and controls 21 of the 350 seats in the Spanish parliament.
The coalition has been plagued by internal squabbling in recent years and its relationship with the Socialists has been far from easy.
Efforts by outspoken leader Anguita to forge closer relations with the PSOE at the last election met a dead end with Socialists complaining that Anguita's demands came with too many strings attached.
